text: I think going through the Alps in a train is one of the most special travel experiences you can do in life. But what happens? A line needs to get to higher altitude, and then to pass the mountain range. So it can't do a straight line, it needs to negotiate through the valley, the tunnels, the curves, the bridges. And then come down safely. It doesn't matter if it's the Glacier Express from St. Moritz to Zermatt, or the Bernina Express going to Italy, or the other line through Gotthard, the general logic is the same. So, it starts normally in a big city, Zurich, Milan, Munich, Vienna. Starts in the big station, goes through the suburbs, through the industry. Follows a river, follows a lake. Then it starts climbing, and slowly the landscape starts closing, the nature starts closing. Fields, then trees, then the mountain. A railway line doesn't like steep gradients, because the friction, adhesion, between the wheel and the rail is not very good. So it goes up very slowly. It goes up in the valley, and turns and turns and turns to gain height. It looks like it's going in a wrong direction, but actually, it's very calculated. And when it goes up, it passes stone viaducts, small tunnels, villages, and the tracks are very close to the village. And then the spiral tunnels, or loop tunnels, where you enter into the mountain, you turn around in the tunnel, and you exit higher. And then you're facing the same valley, but from a different angle. And then, for the steepest gradients, there is the rack railway, where there is a rail in the middle, with teeth, that engages with the train, and it can really go up very steep. But modern railways, they try to avoid that. They want to build huge tunnels through the mountain. Like Gotthard base tunnel, that is 57 km long. That's below the Alps, that goes through the mountain and completely avoids the climb. Then, the line is very complex, and very managed. Because it's always electrified, it's always signalled. It's very difficult to keep the signal and keep the rail working properly in snow, in fog, in rocks. It's very single track, so it needs to pass at stations or in loops. It needs to be scheduled very carefully. There are all these barriers to protect from avalanches, or from rocks falling, from snow. There are snow fences, there are heated switches. And in winter, the team comes and cleans the platforms, and checks the tracks. In summer, there's heat, thunderstorms, that can cause problems. Behind the scenes, there are guys that manage the traffic, because it goes across international borders, so it's very complex to manage. And then you travel in a very panoramic carriage, that has very large curved windows, that lets you see the landscape very easily. And the carriage floats over the landscape. And you see these terraced fields.
